title: Trust, Disclosure, and Conditional Acceptance of Digital Mental Health Support Among Jordanian and Syrian Adolescent Girls: A Qualitative Study
content: Adolescent girls may experience emotional distress arising from the interplay of academic pressures, family dynamics, social expectations, and, for displaced populations, displacement-related adversity; at the same time, stigma, anticipated judgment, concerns about confidentiality, and limited trust may hinder help-seeking. This study explored how Jordanian and Syrian adolescent girls understand emotional distress, navigate disclosure and support, and perceive digital psychological services. An exploratory qualitative design was used. Nine focus group discussions were conducted in Arabic with 39 girls aged 15–19 years, recruited purposively through health and community channels in Jordan. Data were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis across the full dataset while retaining group context to examine shared and context-specific patterns. Three interrelated themes were developed: (1) emotional stress, academic demands, and the weight of expectations; (2) navigating support through informal networks and carefully negotiated boundaries of trust; and (3) strong but conditional interest in digital psychological support. Pressure associated with the high-stakes Tawjihi examination, selective disclosure to trusted family members and friends, and concerns about privacy were prominent, while some Syrian participants additionally described displacement-related uncertainty. Digital support was viewed more favorably when confidentiality, professional credibility, institutional legitimacy, and control over disclosure were assured. Trust emerged as the central organizing concept linking distress, disclosure, help-seeking, and digital-service acceptability, suggesting digital services should prioritize privacy, credibility, and adolescents’ control over engagement.
